title: Plant Physiology
html:
A plant does not move, does not hunt and does not drink.

Yet a single maize plant in a Terai field pulls something like two hundred litres of water out of the soil in a season, loses almost all of it to the air, and builds its entire body out of a gas that makes up four hundredths of one per cent of that air.

This unit is about how.

It is the longest unit in the Botany paper — twenty of your eighty-odd Botany hours — and it is the one that rewards understanding over memorising, because almost every question is a why question wearing a what disguise.

What the examiner asks from this unit

Photosynthesis and respiration together supply most of the marks.

Expect one long question from the pair almost every year — the light reaction and the Z-scheme, the Calvin cycle with its stoichiometry, C3 against C4 against CAM, or the complete aerobic breakdown of glucose with a correct ATP tally.

Water relations supplies the short questions: water potential and its components, ascent of sap, the mechanism of stomatal opening, transpiration versus guttation.

Hormones and movements are small but certain — a four-mark comparison or a one-mark "which hormone does X". Learn the numbers.

ATP counts, RQ values and hormone functions are the only places in this unit where an examiner can mark you wrong without argument.

2.1 Water relation

Ninety per cent of a growing herbaceous plant is water.

It is the solvent every reaction runs in, the reagent that photolysis splits, the pressure that holds a soft stem upright, and the vehicle that carries every mineral ion from soil to leaf.

Water relations is the study of how a plant gets it, moves it and loses it.

Diffusion, imbibition and osmosis

Diffusion is the net movement of particles of a gas, liquid or dissolved solute from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, by their own kinetic energy.

It needs no membrane, no energy input and no living cell. It is how carbon dioxide reaches a mesophyll cell and how oxygen leaves one.

It is fast over micrometres and hopelessly slow over metres — which is exactly why plants need a transport system at all.

Imbibition is the adsorption of water by a hydrophilic colloid, which swells as a result. A dry gram seed dropped in water at night is three times its size by morning; the wooden handle of a khukuri swells and tightens in the monsoon.

Two conditions must be met: there must be an affinity between the imbibant and the liquid, and there must be a water potential gradient between them.

The force developed is the imbibition pressure, and it can be enormous — measured swelling pressures of wood run from about 0.4 to 4 MPa.

Imbibition capacity follows the order protein > starch > cellulose, which is why a pea seed (protein-rich) swells more than a wheat grain (starch-rich).

Imbibition is the first step in seed germination, and the heat released as water molecules bind to the colloid is the heat of wetting.

Osmosis is the net diffusion of water (the solvent) across a selectively permeable membrane, from a solution of higher water potential to one of lower water potential. Osmosis is a special case of diffusion, not a separate process.

In a plant cell the plasma membrane and the tonoplast are the selectively permeable membranes; the cell wall is freely permeable and plays no part in selection.

Common mistake

Do not define osmosis as "movement of water from a dilute to a concentrated solution." That is true only when both solutions are at the same pressure.

The moment you press on one side — and a turgid plant cell is under several atmospheres of pressure — water can move into the more dilute solution. The only definition that always works is the one in terms of water potential.

Water potential and its components

The free energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure free water at the same temperature and atmospheric pressure, is the water potential, \Psi_w (Greek letter psi).

Because the reference state is pure free water, and because anything you do to water — dissolving something in it, putting it under tension, letting it wet a surface — lowers its free energy, the rule is simple:

\Psi_w \text{ of pure free water} = 0

and the water potential of any solution or any cell is negative. Water always moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. The SI unit is the pascal; in practice we use the megapascal (MPa), where 1 MPa = 10 bar = 9.87 atmospheres.

Water potential is a sum of four components:

\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p + \Psi_m + \Psi_g

Component Name Sign What causes it
\Psi_s Solute (osmotic) potential always \le 0 dissolved solutes lowering free energy
\Psi_p Pressure potential usually > 0 in cells, negative in xylem turgor pressure, or tension
\Psi_m Matric potential always \le 0 water bound to walls, colloids, soil particles
\Psi_g Gravitational potential +0.01 MPa per metre of height the weight of the water column

For an ordinary vacuolated cell \Psi_m is small and \Psi_g is ignorable below about ten metres, so the working equation you will use in problems is

\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p

Two of these deserve a second look.

\Psi_p is negative in the xylem — the water there is under tension, being pulled from above, not pushed from below, and a negative pressure potential is the single most important idea in the ascent of sap.

\Psi_m dominates in drying soil and in dry seeds, where measured water potentials of -50 to -350 MPa are routine; that is the gradient that drives imbibition.

Osmotic pressure, turgor and plasmolysis

The osmotic pressure (OP) of a solution is the pressure that must be applied to it to stop water entering it through a selectively permeable membrane.

It is a positive quantity, and it is numerically equal to the solute potential with the sign reversed: \Psi_s = -\text{OP}. For a dilute solution it obeys the van't Hoff equation

\Psi_s = - i\,m\,R\,T

where i is the van't Hoff factor (1 for sucrose or glucose, about 2 for NaCl, about 3 for CaCl_2), m is molality in mol kg^{-1} (molarity is close enough for dilute solutions), R = 0.00831 L MPa mol^{-1} K^{-1} and T is absolute temperature in kelvin.

Solute potential of a sucrose solution

Calculate the solute potential of a 1.0 M sucrose solution at 25 °C.

Sucrose does not ionise, so i = 1. Convert the temperature: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K.

\Psi_s = -(1)(1.0)(0.00831)(298)

\Psi_s = -2.48 \text{ MPa}

Because a solution open to the atmosphere has \Psi_p = 0, the water potential of this solution is also -2.48 MPa. A cell with \Psi_w = -1.2 MPa placed in it would lose water and plasmolyse.

A note for the careful student: the measured value for real 1.0 M sucrose is about -2.7 MPa, because a concentrated sucrose solution is not ideal.

Quote -2.48 MPa as the van't Hoff answer and -2.7 MPa as the measured one — never present the measured figure as the result of the calculation.

When a cell is put in a hypertonic solution it loses water, the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the wall, and the cell is plasmolysed.

The stage at which the protoplast has just begun to pull away — when the wall is exerting no pressure at all, so \Psi_p = 0 — is incipient plasmolysis, and at that moment \Psi_w = \Psi_s.

Operationally it is taken as the external concentration at which half the cells in a peeled onion epidermis show visible plasmolysis; a 0.6 M sucrose solution is the standard.

Returning the cell to water reverses the process — deplasmolysis. Plasmolysis proves that the protoplast is alive and that the membrane is selectively permeable, and it is the only simple way to estimate a cell's solute potential.

Absorption of water by roots

Water enters through the root hair zone and, less obviously, along the whole length of the young root.

A root hair is a tubular extension of a single epiblema cell, with a thin cellulose wall, no cuticle, and a large vacuole whose sap has a water potential more negative than that of the soil solution.

Soil at field capacity sits at about -0.015 MPa; a root hair at perhaps -0.6 MPa; water flows inward.

From the epiblema water crosses the cortex to the xylem by three pathways running in parallel:

  • Apoplast pathway — through the interconnected cell walls and intercellular spaces, never crossing a membrane. Fastest, and the main route in a rapidly transpiring plant.
  • Symplast pathway — from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata, crossing the plasma membrane once at the start.
  • Transmembrane pathway — in and out of each cell in turn across both membranes, through water channels called aquaporins.

At the endodermis the apoplast route is blocked.

The Casparian strip — a band of lignin (with suberin deposited later) in the radial and transverse walls of every endodermal cell — forces water and dissolved ions to cross at least one plasma membrane before they can reach the stele.

That single checkpoint gives the root its selectivity, stops solutes leaking back out, and makes root pressure possible.

Aquaporins are integral membrane proteins forming water-selective pores; Peter Agre received the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering them, and the first plant aquaporin was identified in Arabidopsis in 1993.

They are channels, not pumps — they let water move faster down a gradient, but they cannot move it against one.

Absorption is classified as passive or active. In passive absorption, which accounts for the overwhelming majority of uptake in a transpiring plant, the pull originates in the leaves and the root is a passive absorbing surface.

In "active" absorption the root itself generates the driving force by pumping ions into the xylem, lowering its water potential, so water follows osmotically.

Common mistake

"Active absorption of water" does not mean water is pumped. There is no water pump in any plant. What is active is the transport of ions; water always follows its own potential gradient.

The commonly quoted "96 % passive, 4 % active" split is a teaching heuristic, not a measurement.

Root pressure

If you cut the stem of a well-watered tomato or Colocasia plant near the ground early in the morning, sap wells up from the stump.

Attach a manometer and you can measure the positive hydrostatic pressure developing in the root xylem: root pressure. Stephen Hales measured it first, in a grapevine, in Vegetable Staticks (1727), obtaining about 0.14 MPa.

Root pressure is osmotic in origin.

Endodermal cells actively secrete ions into the xylem; the Casparian strip prevents them leaking back; the xylem sap becomes more concentrated than the surrounding cortical cells; water enters osmotically and, having nowhere else to go, pushes upward.

Typical values are 0.1–0.2 MPa, and a survey of 109 species found a maximum of only 0.148 MPa.

Root pressure cannot explain the ascent of sap, for four reasons that are worth learning as a set:

  1. It is far too small — 0.1 MPa would lift water about ten metres, against the thirty or more that a tall tree needs.
  2. It is greatest at night and in humid weather, and falls to zero or goes negative at midday, exactly when the plant is moving the most water.
  3. It is absent in many gymnosperms; detopped pine and spruce trunks do not exude at all.
  4. Ascent continues perfectly well in stems whose living cells have been killed by poison or heat.

Its real function, in modern physiology, is to refill xylem vessels that have become air-locked (embolised) overnight, and to drive guttation.

Ascent of sap

Water has to climb from root to leaf. In the 115 m Sequoia sempervirens "Hyperion", the tallest tree measured, that is a gravitational cost alone of about 1.15 MPa, plus another 2 MPa or so to overcome friction in the conduits.

Three classes of theory have been offered.

Vital force theories hold that living cells of the stem pump the water up.

Godlewski's relay-pump theory (1884) proposed that xylem parenchyma and medullary ray cells pump in relay; J. C. Bose (1923) proposed that the innermost cortical cells pulsate rhythmically.

Both are dead, killed by Strasburger's experiment (1891–93): twenty-metre oak trunks were stood in picric acid, copper sulphate and boiling water.

The poison rose to the leaves, killing every living cell on the way, and the ascent of sap continued.

A quantitative objection finishes Bose's version — sap would have to pass through 230 to 400 pulsating cells every second, against a pulse period Bose himself gave as about fourteen seconds.

Physical force theories that rely on capillarity also fail, and the arithmetic is worth doing. Capillary rise is h = 2\gamma\cos\theta / \rho g r.

With \gamma = 72.8 mN m^{-1}, a xylem vessel of radius 25 µm gives h \approx 0.6 m; a wide vessel of radius 200 µm gives just 7 cm.

Worse, the theory predicts that the tallest trees should have the narrowest vessels, whereas conduit diameter actually increases towards the base of a tall trunk.

The cohesion–tension theory of Dixon and Joly (preliminary note 1894; full paper, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 1895), proposed independently by Askenasy in the same year, is the accepted explanation. It rests on three pillars:

  • Transpiration pull. Water evaporates from the menisci held in nanometre-scale pores in the mesophyll cell walls — pores of radius 5–10 nm, not from the open cell surfaces. The Laplace relation \Delta P \approx 2\gamma/r shows that such menisci can generate tensions of the order of -30 MPa, far more than any tree requires. The energy comes entirely from the sun as latent heat of vaporisation (2260 kJ per litre); no metabolic energy is spent.
  • Cohesion. Hydrogen bonding between water molecules gives liquid water a tensile strength that has been measured at better than -25 MPa in spinning Z-tubes, so the column does not snap.
  • Adhesion. Hydrogen bonding between water and the lignocellulose of the vessel wall keeps the column attached and prevents it pulling away.

The result is a continuous, cohesive, tense water column — the transpiration–cohesion–tension mechanism — running unbroken from the soil solution to the evaporating surface of the leaf, with the xylem sap under a negative pressure potential of typically -0.5 to -3.0 MPa at midday.

Direct measurement by the pressure chamber and by the centrifuge confirmed sustained negative pressures in 1995, and the xylem-pressure-probe controversy of the 1990s was resolved when it was shown that inserting the probe itself nucleates cavitation.

Transpiration

Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant. Between 97 and 99.5 per cent of all the water a plant absorbs is lost this way. It comes in three kinds:

Type Site Share of total
Stomatal through stomata 80–90 %
Cuticular directly through the cuticle 5–10 % (up to 20–30 % in thin-cuticled mesophytes)
Lenticular through lenticels of woody stems about 0.1 %

The remarkable fact about stomatal transpiration is that stomata occupy only 0.5 to 3 per cent of the leaf surface yet carry almost all the water loss — because diffusion through many small pores is nearly as fast as through one large opening of the same total area.

Transpiration has real benefits: it drives the ascent of sap and with it the bulk movement of mineral ions, and the latent heat carried off cools the leaf by a useful 2–5 °C on a hot Terai afternoon.

It also costs the plant enormously — roughly 400 molecules of water are lost for every molecule of CO_2 fixed in a C3 plant.

Curtis called it a "necessary evil" in 1926, and the phrase has stuck, but the modern framing is better: transpiration is not a process the plant performs, it is the unavoidable price of opening the stomata to let carbon dioxide in.

The transpiration ratio — grams of water transpired per gram of dry matter produced — is about 500 for C3 plants, 250 for C4 plants and 50 for CAM plants (figures vary between textbook editions; quote them as approximations).

The mechanism of stomatal movement

A stoma is a pore bounded by two guard cells.

Unlike ordinary epidermal cells, guard cells contain chloroplasts and have walls of uneven thickness and, crucially, circumferentially arranged cellulose microfibrils — the property called radial micellation.

Because the microfibrils hoop the cell, turgor cannot make the cell fatter; it can only make it longer. The two guard cells are attached to each other at their ends, so as they lengthen they bow apart, and the pore opens.

Opening is driven by potassium influx. The accepted sequence is:

  1. Blue light is absorbed by phototropin receptors in the guard-cell plasma membrane.
  2. This activates the plasma-membrane H^+-ATPase, which pumps protons out and hyperpolarises the membrane to around -150 mV.
  3. The negative interior opens inward-rectifying K^+ channels, and K^+ floods in — guard-cell potassium rises from about 100 mM to 400–800 mM.
  4. Charge is balanced by Cl^- and NO_3^- taken up from outside, and by malate synthesised inside the guard cell by PEP carboxylase from carbon skeletons released by starch breakdown.
  5. The solute potential of the guard cell falls by 0.4–0.8 MPa, water enters osmotically, turgor rises, and radial micellation converts that turgor into opening.

Closing is driven by abscisic acid. Water stress raises ABA, ABA binds its receptors, an anion channel opens, the membrane depolarises, an outward K^+ channel opens, solutes leak out, water follows and the pore shuts.

Common mistake

The modern explanation of stomatal movement is Levitt's active \text{K}^+–\text{H}^+ ion-exchange mechanism, not the older starch–sugar interconversion hypothesis.

Guard cells in onion (Allium cepa) contain no starch at all yet open and close normally using \text{KCl} as the osmoticum; in starch-containing guard cells, starch supplies carbon skeletons for malate, the counter-ion for \text{K}^+.

Common mistake

"Monocots have dumb-bell shaped guard cells" is wrong. Dumb-bell guard cells are a feature of the grass family (Poaceae), and of some sedges — maize, rice, wheat, bamboo.

Non-grass monocots such as onion, Tradescantia, lilies and orchids have ordinary kidney-shaped guard cells.

Grass stomata open and close faster because of their geometry and because they work as an ionic see-saw with a pair of subsidiary cells.

Factors affecting transpiration

External factors. Light opens stomata and so raises transpiration. Temperature raises it steeply, because it raises the saturation vapour pressure of the air inside the leaf. Atmospheric humidity lowers it.

Wind is biphasic — a breeze thins the boundary layer of still, humid air over the leaf and raises transpiration, but a strong wind eventually causes stomatal closure and the rate falls again.

Soil water availability is the ultimate limit.

Relative humidity is the wrong variable

The driving force for evaporation is the vapour pressure deficit (VPD), not relative humidity. At 50 % RH the VPD is 0.61 kPa at 10 °C but 3.69 kPa at 40 °C — a six-fold difference at identical relative humidity.

That is why a plant wilts on a hot dry Terai afternoon and not on a cool humid Kathmandu morning at the same RH reading.

Internal factors. Total leaf area; thickness of the cuticle and the wax layer; trichomes, which trap a humid boundary layer; sunken stomata buried in pits, as in Nerium; leaf rolling by bulliform cells in grasses; stomatal frequency, typically 100–1000 per mm^2; and the distribution of stomata — most leaves are hypostomatous (stomata on the lower surface only), grasses are amphistomatous, and the floating leaf of Nymphaea is epistomatous, with stomata only on top.

Antitranspirants are substances applied to reduce transpiration: stomatal-closing types such as phenylmercuric acetate and ABA; film-forming types such as wax emulsions and pinolene; and reflectants such as kaolin.

All share the same limitation — CO_2 and H_2O share the same pore, so cutting water loss cuts photosynthesis roughly in proportion, and the leaf runs hotter.

Guttation

Guttation is the exudation of liquid water — not vapour — from the margins and tips of intact leaves, through specialised pores called hydathodes. The word is from the Latin gutta, a drop, and was coined by Burgerstein in 1887.

A hydathode is a modified region at a vein ending.

Working outward: the tracheids of the vein end blindly in a mass of loosely packed, chlorophyll-poor parenchyma called the epithem, which is enclosed by a sheath and opens to the outside through one or more water pores.

A water pore is a modified stoma — larger than an ordinary stoma and permanently open, having lost the power of movement.

Guttation happens when root pressure is high and transpiration is low: at night and in the early morning, in moist soil and humid air.

The classic demonstration plant is Colocasia esculenta (pidalu, taro), which can exude 5 to 300 mL from a single leaf in one night; grasses, tomato, strawberry, Tropaeolum and Fuchsia do it too. Most conifers do not.

Guttation Dew
Origin of the water internal — xylem sap external — atmospheric vapour
Driving force root pressure cooling of the surface below dew point
Exit site hydathodes at margins and tips anywhere, including stones and metal
Composition dilute solution of salts, sugars, amino acids essentially pure water
Residue on drying a white crust none

Distinguish both from bleeding, which is the exudation of sap from a cut or injured surface — the flow from a tapped Borassus inflorescence or a pruned grapevine.

2.2 Photosynthesis

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to reduce carbon dioxide to carbohydrate, with water as the electron donor and oxygen as a by-product.

It is the only significant entry point of energy into the biosphere, and every gram of food in every kitchen in Nepal traces back to it.

The overall equation is written best as

6 CO₂ + 12 H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ + 6 H₂O (in light, in the presence of chlorophyll)

Twelve water molecules appear on the left, not six, because all of the oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide.

Van Niel predicted this from the chemistry of photosynthetic bacteria, and Ruben, Randall, Kamen and Hyde proved it in 1941 by supplying Chlorella with water labelled with the heavy isotope ^{18}O and recovering the label in the oxygen gas.

The site: the chloroplast

The chloroplast is a double-membrane-bounded plastid. Inside the inner membrane is the stroma, a protein-rich matrix containing the enzymes of carbon fixation, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and starch grains.

Suspended in the stroma is a third, quite separate membrane system: flattened sacs called thylakoids, stacked into piles called grana (singular granum) and connected between stacks by stroma lamellae (intergranal thylakoids).

The space enclosed by the thylakoid membrane is the lumen.

That three-compartment design is the whole point. The pigments and electron carriers sit in the thylakoid membrane; protons are pumped into the lumen; the enzymes that use the products sit in the stroma.

Remember the rule: light reaction in the thylakoid, dark reaction in the stroma.

The photosynthetic pigments fall into three groups.

Chlorophyll a (blue-green, \text{C}_{55}\text{H}_{72}\text{O}_5\text{N}_4\text{Mg}) is the only pigment that can convert light into chemical energy; it is the primary or reaction-centre pigment.

Chlorophyll b, the carotenes (orange) and the xanthophylls (yellow) are accessory pigments: they absorb wavelengths chlorophyll a misses and transfer the energy to it, and carotenoids additionally protect the reaction centre from photo-oxidation.

Chlorophyll absorbs strongly in the blue and the red and reflects green, which is why leaves are green.

The light reaction

Light energy is absorbed by two pigment assemblies, each an antenna of a few hundred pigment molecules funnelling energy into a single special pair of chlorophyll a molecules:

  • Photosystem II (PS II), reaction centre P680 — named for its absorption maximum at 680 nm. Found mostly in the grana.
  • Photosystem I (PS I), reaction centre P700 — absorption maximum 700 nm. Found mostly in the stroma lamellae and at granal margins.
Common mistake

P680 and P700 are both chlorophyll a. The numbers are wavelengths in nanometres, not molecular differences. And despite its name, PS II acts first in the chain — it was simply discovered second.

Non-cyclic photophosphorylation is the main pathway. Electrons travel one way, from water to NADP^+, through the famous Z-scheme:

Trace it in words. Light strikes PS II; P680 is excited to P680* and loses an electron to pheophytin.

The electron passes to plastoquinone (\text{Q}_A, \text{Q}_B, then the PQ pool), to the cytochrome b_6f complex, to the copper protein plastocyanin, and so to PS I. Meanwhile P680^+ — the strongest oxidising agent known in biology, at about +1.2 V — is so electron-hungry that it can tear electrons out of water.

Light then excites P700 to P700*, which passes its electron through \text{A}_0, phylloquinone and a chain of iron–sulphur centres to ferredoxin, and finally the enzyme ferredoxin–NADP^+ reductase (FNR) uses it to reduce NADP^+ to NADPH.

Photolysis of water happens at the oxygen-evolving complex, a cluster of four manganese, one calcium and five oxygen atoms (\text{Mn}_4\text{CaO}_5) on the lumen side of PS II, which also needs chloride:

2\,\text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\,\text{H}^+ + 4\,e^-

Common mistake

The oxygen-evolving complex faces the thylakoid lumen. All four protons (4\text{H}^+) from photolysis of water are released into the lumen, directly building the proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis.

The protons accumulating in the lumen — four per two water molecules from photolysis, plus four more pumped across by the cytochrome b_6f complex — create a proton gradient.

They escape through ATP synthase, whose stalk projects into the stroma, and their passage drives the phosphorylation of ADP.

This is chemiosmosis, and because the phosphorylation is ultimately driven by light it is called photophosphorylation.

Cyclic photophosphorylation uses PS I alone. The electron from ferredoxin, instead of going to NADP^+, is fed back into the plastoquinone pool and returns to P700 through cytochrome b_6f.

Protons are still pumped, so ATP is made — but no NADPH, and no oxygen, because water is never split.

Non-cyclic Cyclic
Photosystems PS II and PS I PS I only
Electron path open — water to NADP^+ closed loop
Electron donor water the electron returns; none needed
Products ATP + NADPH + O_2 ATP only
Photolysis yes no
Main location grana thylakoids stroma lamellae

Why keep both? Because the Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH in a ratio of exactly 3 : 2 (= 1.50), while linear electron flow delivers them at about 1.28. Cyclic flow makes up the ATP shortfall.

This is the answer to "what is the significance of cyclic photophosphorylation," and it is worth more than the usual vague line about "extra ATP".

The dark reaction: the Calvin cycle

The dark reaction is light-independent, not nocturnal.

It is a cycle of enzyme-catalysed reactions in the stroma, worked out by Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson and James Bassham using ^{14}C and paper chromatography; Calvin received the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Because the first stable product is a three-carbon acid, plants using it alone are called C3 plants.

The cycle has three phases.

1. Carboxylation. The five-carbon acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) combines with CO_2, catalysed by ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO).

The unstable six-carbon intermediate splits at once into two molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA) — the first stable product.

RuBisCO is a sixteen-subunit enzyme (\text{L}_8\text{S}_8), the most abundant protein on Earth, and remarkably slow, turning over only 3 to 10 molecules of CO_2 per second. A plant compensates by making colossal quantities of it.

2. Reduction. Each 3-PGA is phosphorylated by ATP to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, then reduced by NADPH to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P), a triose phosphate. This is the only reduction step and the only place NADPH is used.

3. Regeneration. Most of the G3P is reshuffled through a series of 4-, 5-, 6- and 7-carbon sugar phosphates to rebuild RuBP, a step that costs one more ATP each (at phosphoribulokinase).

The stoichiometry of the Calvin cycle

How many ATP and NADPH are needed to make one molecule of glucose?

Fixing one CO_2 gives two 3-PGA. Each 3-PGA costs 1 ATP (phosphoglycerate kinase) and 1 NADPH (G3P dehydrogenase). So per CO_2 the reduction phase costs 2 ATP and 2 NADPH. Regeneration costs a further 1 ATP per CO_2.

Per CO_2: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH.

Glucose has six carbons, so six turns are needed:

6 \times 3 = 18 \text{ ATP} \qquad 6 \times 2 = 12 \text{ NADPH}

6 CO_2 + 18 ATP + 12 NADPH → 1 glucose. Twelve G3P are produced in those six turns; two leave the cycle to build the hexose and ten are recycled to regenerate the six RuBP.

Note the ATP NADPH ratio of 18 : 12 = 3 : 2.

Photorespiration

RuBisCO's second name — oxygenase — is its weakness.

The active site cannot fully discriminate between CO_2 and O_2, and in ordinary air, where oxygen is some 500 times more abundant than carbon dioxide, RuBP is sometimes oxygenated instead of carboxylated.

The products are one 3-PGA and one molecule of 2-phosphoglycolate, which is useless.

Salvaging it consumes ATP and runs a loop through three organelles — chloroplast, peroxisome (where glycolate oxidase makes hydrogen peroxide, destroyed by catalase) and mitochondrion (where two glycines condense to serine, releasing CO_2 and ammonia).

The cost: one CO_2 is lost for every two oxygenation events, about a quarter of the carbon that enters the pathway. Photorespiration consumes O_2 and releases CO_2 in the light, with no ATP gain — hence the name.

It gets worse as temperature rises and as stomata close, because closed stomata let internal CO_2 fall and internal O_2 rise.

C4 plants and the Hatch–Slack pathway

Some tropical grasses solve the RuBisCO problem by concentrating CO_2 around the enzyme. Hatch and Slack described the pathway in sugarcane in 1966.

C4 leaves have Kranz anatomy (German Kranz, a wreath): the vascular bundles are surrounded by a ring of large, thick-walled bundle-sheath cells packed with chloroplasts, and outside that a ring of mesophyll cells.

The sequence: in the mesophyll cytosol, atmospheric CO_2 is first converted to bicarbonate and fixed by PEP carboxylase onto phosphoenolpyruvate, giving oxaloacetate, a four-carbon acid — hence "C4", and hence the first stable product being OAA, not 3-PGA.

OAA is reduced to malate, which travels through plasmodesmata into the bundle sheath, where it is decarboxylated.

The released CO_2 accumulates to 10–20 times atmospheric concentration around RuBisCO, which now works at near its maximum rate with almost no oxygenation.

The pyruvate returns to the mesophyll and is regenerated to PEP by pyruvate phosphate dikinase.

Two facts make C4 work. PEP carboxylase has no oxygenase activity at all and a far higher affinity for its substrate than RuBisCO. And the whole scheme is a spatial separation: two cell types, two carboxylations.

The extra cost is real. Regenerating PEP by PPDK produces AMP, not ADP, so restoring it takes two ATP equivalents. C4 photosynthesis therefore costs 5 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO_2 — 30 ATP per glucose, against the C3 plant's 18.

CAM plants

Crassulacean acid metabolism solves the same problem by temporal separation instead.

At night, when the air is cool and humid, the stomata open; PEP carboxylase fixes CO_2 to oxaloacetate and then malate, which is stored as malic acid in the large central vacuole — which is why a ghiukumari (Aloe vera) leaf tastes sour at dawn and bland at dusk.

By day the stomata shut tight; the malic acid moves out of the vacuole, is decarboxylated, and the CO_2 released behind closed stomata is fixed by RuBisCO in the ordinary Calvin cycle.

C3 C4 CAM
First stable product 3-PGA (3C) oxaloacetate (4C) oxaloacetate (4C)
Primary CO_2 acceptor RuBP PEP PEP

Factors affecting photosynthesis

Blackman's Law of Limiting Factors (1905): when a process is governed by several factors, its rate is limited by the factor that is in shortest supply. Raise that one and the rate rises until some other factor becomes limiting in turn.

Light. Rate rises with intensity and then saturates.

The light compensation point is the intensity at which photosynthesis exactly balances respiration, so net gas exchange is zero — about 10–50 µmol m^{-2} s^{-1} for a shade plant, over 100 for a sun plant.

Quality matters too: red and blue light are most effective, green least.

Carbon dioxide. Usually the limiting factor in the field. Atmospheric CO_2 is now about 427 ppm (0.043 %) — do not write 0.03 %, which was true in the 1950s.

The CO_2 compensation point is where uptake balances release: 40–100 ppm in C3 plants, only 3–10 ppm in C4 plants, which is exactly why maize outgrows wheat in hot bright weather.

Temperature. Photosynthesis is enzyme-driven, so the rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise up to an optimum, then falls steeply as enzymes denature.

Water, minerals and chlorophyll. Water shortage closes the stomata and cuts off CO_2 long before it affects the biochemistry. Magnesium is in the chlorophyll ring; nitrogen is in the porphyrin and in RuBisCO; iron and manganese are needed to build the electron chain.

Which factor is limiting?

A rice plant is photosynthesising at 20 °C in bright sunlight with the CO_2 concentration held at 420 ppm. The rate does not increase when the light is doubled, but doubles when the CO_2 is raised to 800 ppm. What is limiting, and what would happen if the temperature were raised to 30 °C at 800 ppm?

Doubling the light changes nothing, so light is not limiting — the plant is already light-saturated. Raising CO_2 doubles the rate, so CO_2 is the limiting factor.

At 800 ppm, CO_2 is no longer in short supply, so the next factor in line takes over.

Since enzymes are involved and 20 °C is below the optimum for rice, raising the temperature to 30 °C should raise the rate further — temperature is now limiting.

This is exactly Blackman's principle: the rate is set by whichever single factor is nearest its minimum.

2.3 Respiration

Respiration is the controlled, stepwise oxidation of organic food inside living cells to release energy in a usable form.

The point of the many steps is control: burning glucose in a flame releases the same energy, but all at once and all as heat. A cell releases it in small packets and traps much of it in ATP, the universal energy currency.

\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\,\text{O}_2 \longrightarrow 6\,\text{CO}_2 + 6\,\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{energy}

The standard free-energy change is about -2870 kJ per mole of glucose. Aerobic respiration has four stages.

Glycolysis

Glycolysis (the Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway) happens in the cytoplasm, needs no oxygen, and occurs in every living cell.

Glucose is phosphorylated twice — an investment of 2 ATP, at hexokinase and at phosphofructokinase, the committed and rate-limiting step — then split into two three-carbon triose phosphates.

Each is oxidised (producing NADH at glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) and then yields two ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, at phosphoglycerate kinase and at pyruvate kinase.

Gross yield 4 ATP, investment 2 ATP: net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose, ending in two molecules of pyruvate.

The link reaction

Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix and is handled by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which needs thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD^+, coenzyme A and Mg^{2+}. Each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO_2, is oxidised, and is attached to coenzyme A:

pyruvate (3C) + NAD⁺ + CoA → acetyl-CoA (2C) + CO₂ + NADH

Per glucose this gives 2 CO_2 + 2 NADH. The reaction is irreversible — which is why animals and plants cannot convert fat back into sugar by simply reversing it.

The Krebs cycle

Also called the citric acid cycle or tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, described by Hans Krebs in 1937 (Nobel Prize 1953). It runs in the matrix.

Acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with oxaloacetate (4C) to give citrate (6C).

The cycle then runs: citrate → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (5C) → succinyl-CoA (4C) → succinate → fumarate → malate → oxaloacetate, regenerated and ready for the next acetyl-CoA.

The two carbons that entered leave as CO_2 at the two decarboxylations, at isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

Per turn: 3 NADH, 1 FADH_2, 1 ATP (in plants, made directly as ATP), 2 CO_2. Per glucose the cycle turns twice: 6 NADH, 2 FADH_2, 2 ATP, 4 CO_2.

Running total before the electron transport system: 10 NADH, 2 FADH_2, 4 ATP, 6 CO_2. Notice that all six carbons of glucose have now left as carbon dioxide, and not one molecule of oxygen has been used yet.

The electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

The reduced coenzymes are cashed in at the inner mitochondrial membrane, whose infoldings — cristae — provide the enormous surface area needed. Four complexes and two mobile carriers pass electrons downhill in energy:

Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) → ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) → Complex III (cytochrome bc_1) → cytochrome c → Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) → oxygen.

FADH_2 enters at Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase), bypassing Complex I. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor, combining with electrons and protons to form water — which is why you die without it, and why the whole of the Krebs cycle grinds to a halt in its absence.

As electrons pass, Complexes I, III and IV pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. Per pair of electrons: Complex I pumps 4, Complex III pumps 4, Complex IV pumps 2 — so 10 H^+ per NADH and 6 H^+ per FADH_2.

The protons return through ATP synthase (\text{F}_1\text{F}_0 particles), and their flow drives ATP synthesis. This is Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis (Nobel Prize 1978).

Why 38 and why 30–32

Older books state a yield of 38 ATP per glucose. That number came from the pre-chemiosmotic assumption that each NADH must yield a whole number of ATP — 3, and each FADH_2 exactly 2.

Once Mitchell showed that ATP synthesis is driven by a proton gradient, there was no reason for the ratio to be a whole number at all.

Modern accounting: about 4 H^+ are consumed per ATP made (three to turn the rotor and one to carry the phosphate in). So

\text{P/O for NADH} = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5 \qquad \text{P/O for FADH}_2 = \frac{6}{4} = 1.5

The modern ATP tally

But the 2 NADH made in glycolysis are in the cytoplasm, and NADH cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Their electrons must be ferried in by a shuttle:

  • Malate–aspartate shuttle — electrons arrive as NADH at Complex I, worth 2.5 each → 32 ATP.
  • Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle — electrons arrive at the ubiquinone pool, worth only 1.5 each → 32 − 2 = 30 ATP.

Hence the modern answer: 30 to 32 ATP per glucose, with the real figure in a living cell lower still, because some of the proton gradient leaks and some is spent driving transport. Quote 38 only as the classical figure, and say why it is wrong.

Plants complicate the tally further.

Their mitochondria carry external and internal NAD(P)H dehydrogenases that feed electrons into the chain without pumping any protons, and a cyanide-resistant alternative oxidase (AOX) that passes electrons from ubiquinol straight to oxygen, bypassing Complexes III and IV entirely and releasing the energy as heat.

That is how the spadix of Arum warms itself by 10 °C or more to volatilise the scents that attract its pollinators.

Anaerobic respiration and fermentation

Without oxygen the electron transport system stops, NADH cannot be reoxidised, and glycolysis would halt for want of NAD^+. Fermentation exists to regenerate NAD^+ so that glycolysis can continue.

Alcoholic fermentation, in yeast and in flooded plant roots: pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate decarboxylase to acetaldehyde, which is reduced by alcohol dehydrogenase to ethanol.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + energy

Lactic acid fermentation, in overworked muscle and in Lactobacillus: pyruvate is reduced directly by lactate dehydrogenase, with no CO_2 released.

C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid) + energy

Common mistake

Fermentation itself yields zero ATP. The 2 ATP per glucose that anaerobic respiration nets all come from glycolysis.

The free-energy change of alcoholic fermentation is about -235 kJ mol^{-1} against -2870 for aerobic respiration — only about 8 % of the available energy is released, and the rest stays locked in the ethanol.

That is why yeast makes alcohol and why anaerobic organisms must eat so much.

The Pasteur effect is the observation that glucose consumption falls sharply when a fermenting culture is given oxygen — ATP and citrate accumulate and inhibit phosphofructokinase, throttling glycolysis back.

Respiratory quotient

The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of the volume of carbon dioxide evolved to the volume of oxygen consumed in the same time. It is measured with a Ganong's respirometer, and it tells you what substrate is being respired.

\text{RQ} = \frac{\text{volume of CO}_2 \text{ evolved}}{\text{volume of O}_2 \text{ consumed}}

Balance the equation for complete oxidation. Two molecules are needed to balance the hydrogens in whole numbers:

Fats are poor in oxygen relative to carbon, so oxidising them needs a great deal of external oxygen and the RQ falls below 1. Organic acids are the opposite — already oxygen-rich — so they need little oxygen and the RQ rises above 1.

That single idea explains the whole table.

2.4 Plant hormones

A plant hormone (phytohormone, plant growth regulator) is an organic substance produced in small quantities in one part of a plant, transported to another part, where it regulates a physiological process.

Plants have no glands and no nervous system; hormones are the whole of their long-distance chemical coordination.

Auxin

Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) is the principal natural auxin, made from the amino acid tryptophan, chiefly in the shoot apical meristem, young leaves and developing seeds.

The discovery is a chain of four experiments, and examiners like it:

  1. Charles and Francis Darwin (1880), in The Power of Movement in Plants, covered the tips of canary-grass coleoptiles and found that they no longer bent towards light, while covering the lower part made no difference. The tip perceives the light; the bending happens below it. They inferred that some "influence" is transmitted downward.
  2. Boysen-Jensen (1913) cut off the tip and replaced it on a block of gelatin. Bending still occurred, so the influence is a chemical that can diffuse.
  3. Paál (1918) replaced a severed tip off-centre, in complete darkness, and got curvature anyway — proving that the chemical, not the light, causes the bending.
  4. Went (1926–28) let the substance diffuse out of severed tips into agar blocks, applied the blocks to decapitated Avena coleoptiles, and found curvature proportional to concentration. He named the substance auxin and gave us the Avena curvature bioassay.

Auxin moves by polar transport, cell to cell, basipetally in the shoot, driven by efflux carrier proteins.

Its functions: cell elongation, apical dominance (auxin from the apex suppresses the axillary buds below — which is exactly why plucking the tip of a tea bush makes it branch), root initiation on cuttings, prevention of pre-harvest fruit and leaf fall, parthenocarpy, and the formation of the abscission layer at high concentration.

Synthetic auxins include IBA and NAA (rooting hormones), 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T. As weedkillers they are selective against dicots, which is why 2,4-D kills broadleaf weeds in a rice or wheat field while leaving the crop untouched.

Common mistake

Auxin's dose–response is bell-shaped, and roots and shoots have wildly different optima.

A concentration that gives maximum stem elongation (10^{-5} M) strongly inhibits root growth; roots are promoted only around 10^{-10}–10^{-8} M. "Auxin promotes growth" is only half a sentence.

Gibberellin

Gibberellic acid (GA_3) is the best known of over a hundred and thirty gibberellins, though only a handful are biologically active.

The story begins with bakanae or "foolish seedling" disease of rice, in which infected seedlings grow tall, pale and spindly and then collapse.

Kurosawa (1926) showed that a cell-free filtrate of the fungus reproduced the symptoms; Yabuta and Sumiki (1938) crystallised the substance. The fungus is Gibberella fujikuroi (anamorph Fusarium fujikuroi).

Functions: internode elongation (a GA-treated dwarf pea grows as tall as a normal one), bolting — the sudden elongation of the stem in rosette plants like cabbage and beet before flowering — breaking of seed and bud dormancy, induction of α-amylase in the barley aleurone layer during germination (the basis of commercial malting), and delay of senescence in citrus.

Commercially it is sprayed on Thompson Seedless grapes to enlarge the berries and loosen the bunch.

Cytokinin

Kinetin (N^6-furfuryladenine) was isolated by Miller and Skoog (1955) from autoclaved herring sperm DNA; it is an artefact of DNA breakdown and not a normal plant constituent.

The first genuine natural cytokinin was zeatin, isolated by Letham (1963) from the milky endosperm of maize. Cytokinins are adenine derivatives, made chiefly in the root apex and carried upward in the xylem.

Functions: promotion of cytokinesis (cell division — but only in the presence of auxin), breaking of bud dormancy, counteraction of apical dominance by promoting lateral bud growth, and delay of leaf senescence, known as the Richmond–Lang effect.

The tissue-culture ratio — get the direction right

In plant tissue culture the ratio of auxin to cytokinin determines what the callus becomes:

  • High auxin : low cytokinin → roots
  • High cytokinin : low auxin → shoots
  • Roughly equal → undifferentiated callus

This is Skoog and Miller's 1957 result, and it is the most commonly inverted fact in the whole chapter.

Abscisic acid

ABA was found twice at once — as abscisin II by Addicott's group working on cotton boll abscission, and as dormin by Wareing's group working on bud dormancy in sycamore — and the two proved identical.

It is a sesquiterpenoid, but in plants it is made by cleaving a carotenoid (violaxanthin, then 9-cis-neoxanthin) by the enzyme NCED.

ABA is the stress hormone, the general growth inhibitor and the antagonist of gibberellin.

Its functions: closure of stomata under water stress (its single most important role), induction and maintenance of seed dormancy and seed maturation, inhibition of germination, and promotion of senescence.

Common mistake

Despite the name, ABA is not the hormone of abscission in most plants. It got its name from the cotton bolls it was first isolated from. Leaf and fruit abscission is regulated mainly by ethylene; auxin delays it.

If a question asks which hormone causes leaf fall, the answer is ethylene.

Ethylene

Ethylene (C_2H_4) is the only gaseous plant hormone.

Neljubow (1901) traced the stunting of pea seedlings near gas lamps to ethylene in the illuminating gas, and described the triple response — inhibition of stem elongation, radial swelling of the stem, and horizontal growth.

Gane (1934) proved that apples themselves produce it. It is made from the amino acid methionine, via SAM and then ACC, the immediate precursor.

Functions: ripening of fruits, senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers, epinasty (the downward curving of tomato leaves in waterlogged soil), breaking of dormancy, induction of flowering in pineapple and mango, and promotion of female flowers in cucurbits.

Fruit ripening deserves a paragraph of its own.

Climacteric fruits — banana, mango, papaya, tomato, apple, guava — show a sudden burst of ethylene and a matching surge of respiration at the onset of ripening, and this burst is autocatalytic: ethylene stimulates its own production, so one ripe fruit ripens its neighbours.

That is "one bad apple spoils the barrel", and it is why ripe fruit is packed with green fruit in a closed basket.

Non-climacteric fruits — orange, grape, litchi, strawberry, pineapple — have no such burst and will never ripen properly once picked.

Commercially, ethylene is supplied as ethephon (ethrel), a liquid that releases ethylene inside the plant.

Common mistake

The calcium carbide widely used to ripen mangoes and bananas in South Asian markets does not release ethylene.

It releases acetylene, a weak mimic which de-greens the peel without properly developing the sugars and flavour, so the fruit looks ripe and tastes of nothing.

The real danger is the impurities in technical-grade carbide, which release phosphine and arsine. Carbide ripening is banned in India and prohibited in Nepal; controlled ethylene gas in a ripening chamber is the legal method.

2.5 Plant growth and movement

Growth

Growth is a permanent and irreversible increase in size, volume or dry weight of an organism or its parts, accompanied by metabolic activity.

The word irreversible does the work: a wilted leaf that swells again after watering has not grown, because the change was reversible turgor, not new material.

Growth in plants is localised, confined to the meristems, and indeterminate — a tree keeps adding new organs for as long as it lives.

The growing region of a root or shoot has three zones, running back from the tip: the zone of cell division (the meristem proper), the zone of cell elongation, where most of the measurable lengthening occurs, and the zone of maturation or differentiation, where cells take on their final form.

Growth is measured with an auxanometer. In the simple arc auxanometer the growing shoot tip is tied to a thread passing over a pulley carrying a long pointer that sweeps across a calibrated arc; the ratio of the pointer arm to the pulley radius magnifies the movement.

Plotted against time, growth follows a sigmoid (S-shaped) curve, called the grand period of growth, with four phases.

Two ways of describing growth rate matter. Arithmetic growth occurs when, of two daughter cells, only one continues to divide while the other differentiates; length increases linearly, L_t = L_0 + rt.

Geometric growth occurs when both daughters divide, giving exponential increase, W_1 = W_0 e^{rt}, where r is the relative growth rate. Real growth is geometric early and arithmetic later, which is what produces the sigmoid shape.

Absolute growth rate is the total increase per unit time. Relative growth rate is the increase per unit of initial size per unit time — the only fair way to compare a seedling with a sapling.

Movement

Plants move. They cannot walk, but parts of them change position, and the movements fall into two great classes.

Tropic movements (tropisms) are growth movements in which the direction of the response is determined by the direction of the stimulus. They result from unequal elongation on the two sides of an organ.

Tropism Stimulus Response
Phototropism light shoot positive, root negative
Geotropism (gravitropism) gravity root positive, shoot negative
Hydrotropism water root positive; overrides gravitropism in dry soil
Chemotropism chemical pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule
Thigmotropism touch/contact tendril of Cucurbita or pea coils round a support

Gravity is perceived by statoliths — dense, starch-filled amyloplasts that settle under gravity in special cells called statocytes, which in a root are the columella cells of the root cap.

The Cholodny–Went hypothesis (1927–28) explains the response: gravity or light causes auxin to be redistributed laterally, and the unequal auxin causes unequal growth.

Common mistake

In a horizontally placed seedling, gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the lower side of both the root and the shoot.

The shoot bends upward and the root bends downward because roots and shoots have different sensitivity thresholds to auxin—the concentration that stimulates cell elongation on the lower side of the shoot inhibits cell elongation on the lower side of the root.

Nastic movements (nasties) are movements in which the direction of the response is fixed by the structure of the organ and is independent of the direction of the stimulus.

Some are growth movements; some are reversible turgor (variation) movements and involve no growth at all.

Mimosa pudica — lajjawati, the sensitive plant — is the classic example and deserves the detail. At the base of each leaflet, each pinna and the whole petiole is a swollen cushion of thin-walled cells called a pulvinus.

When a leaflet is touched, mechanically sensitive channels fire an electrical signal — a genuine action potential — that travels along the leaf at one to three centimetres per second.

When it reaches a pulvinus, the motor cells on the lower (ventral) side suddenly lose K^+ and anions; water follows osmotically; those cells go flaccid while the upper cells stay turgid; and the leaflet folds or the petiole drops.

Folding takes one to three seconds; recovery takes ten to thirty minutes.

Common mistake

Mimosa's response is seismonasty — a nastic, turgor (variation) movement — not thigmotropism and not a growth movement. Nothing grows and nothing is permanent; the leaf returns to exactly where it was.

Thigmotropism is the tendril, which really does grow unequally and really is permanent. Confusing the two is one of the easiest marks to throw away in this unit.

  • Aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH) → link reaction (2 CO_2 + 2 NADH) → Krebs (4 CO_2, 6 NADH, 2 FADH_2, 2 ATP) → ETS.   • Five hormones: auxin (elongation, apical dominance), gibberellin (internode elongation, bolting, α-amylase), cytokinin (cell division, delays senescence; high cytokinin gives shoots), ABA (stomatal closure, dormancy — not abscission), ethylene (fruit ripening, abscission, epinasty).

Model answer D1: the cohesion–tension theory of the ascent of sap (10 marks)

Introduction. The ascent of sap is the upward movement of water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves through the xylem.

A tree must lift water against gravity, which costs about 0.01 MPa for every metre of height, and against the friction of the narrow xylem tubes. For a 100 m tree the total is nearly 3 MPa, far more than a living pump could supply.

The cohesion–tension theory of Dixon and Joly (1895) explains this.

The theory in six points.

  1. Transpiration pull is the engine. Water evaporates from the wet walls of mesophyll cells into the air spaces of the leaf. The water surface in the tiny wall pores (radius 5–10 nm) curves into menisci, and surface tension pulls on the water behind it, creating a tension (negative pressure) that can reach −30 MPa.
  2. Cohesion holds the column together. Water molecules attract each other by hydrogen bonds. A thin column in a xylem tube has a measured tensile strength of more than −25 MPa, so it behaves like a stretched thread.
  3. Adhesion anchors the column. Water also sticks to the cellulose and lignin of the xylem wall, so the column does not slip back or tear away from the wall.
  4. The xylem is a low-resistance pipe. Mature vessels and tracheids are dead, hollow, lignified cells joined end to end, so the tension passes down to the root hairs without a living barrier.
  5. The root only supplies water. The tension in the xylem lowers the water potential of the root, so water flows in from the soil along the water-potential gradient. The energy comes from the sun, not from the plant.
  6. Evidence. The trunk shrinks slightly in diameter at midday as the tension pulls the walls inward; a pressure bomb measures negative sap pressure in a cut shoot; and ultrasonic clicks are heard when a column breaks (cavitation) and air enters.
Theory Claim Why it fails
Root pressure Roots push water up Only 0.1–0.2 MPa, enough for 10–20 m; absent at midday and in many conifers
Vital force (Godlewski, Bose) Living cells pump the water Sap still rises in stems whose living cells are killed by heat or poison (Strasburger)
Capillarity Narrow tubes raise water Gives only about 0.6 m in a 25 µm vessel; wider vessels in taller trees

Conclusion. Only the cohesion–tension theory explains the rise of water to the top of Sal and Chir pine trees of Nepal, because it needs no living cells and no energy from the plant except that supplied by the sun's heat.

Model answer D2: C3, C4 and CAM photosynthesis compared (10 marks)

Introduction. In most plants (C3) the enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO_2 into 3-phosphoglyceric acid.

RuBisCO also binds O_2, which starts photorespiration, a wasteful process that releases CO_2 and can cost up to 25–30% of fixed carbon in hot, dry weather. C4 and CAM plants have evolved two different ways to avoid it.

How C4 plants avoid it (spatial separation). In leaves with Kranz anatomy, the mesophyll cells surround a ring of bundle-sheath cells.

In the mesophyll, PEP carboxylase, which cannot bind O_2, fixes CO_2 into the 4-carbon oxaloacetate, which becomes malate.

The malate moves into the bundle sheath and is decarboxylated, raising the CO_2 concentration around RuBisCO 10–20 times.

The Calvin cycle then runs in almost no oxygen competition, and the 3-carbon pyruvate returns to regenerate PEP at a cost of 2 ATP.

How CAM plants avoid it (temporal separation). Succulents keep stomata closed by day to save water and open them at night.

At night PEP carboxylase fixes CO_2 into malic acid stored in the vacuole, which is why the sap is acidic in the morning.

By day the malic acid is decarboxylated inside the closed leaf, and the released CO_2 is fixed by the Calvin cycle using light energy.

Model answer D3: aerobic respiration and the ATP yield of one glucose (10 marks)

Introduction. Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely to CO_2 and H_2O using oxygen: C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6 O_2 → 6 CO_2 + 6 H_2O + energy. The energy is trapped as ATP in four stages.

  1. Glycolysis (cytoplasm). Glucose (6 C) is split into two pyruvate (3 C). Two ATP are used at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase, and four are made by substrate-level phosphorylation, so the net gain is 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.
  2. Link reaction (mitochondrial matrix). Each pyruvate is decarboxylated and oxidised by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex to acetyl-CoA, giving 1 NADH and 1 CO_2. For one glucose this is 2 NADH and 2 CO_2.
  3. Krebs cycle (matrix). Each acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate to form citrate and is oxidised in eight steps. One turn gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH_2, 1 ATP (or GTP) and 2 CO_2; two turns give 6 NADH, 2 FADH_2, 2 ATP and 4 CO_2.
  4. Electron transport system (inner mitochondrial membrane). NADH and FADH_2 pass electrons through complexes I–IV to oxygen. Protons pumped into the intermembrane space return through ATP synthase, which makes ATP (oxidative phosphorylation). Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water.

Why 38 and why 30–32. The older figure used whole-number P/O ratios of 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH_2. About 10 H^+ are pumped per NADH and about 4 H^+ are needed per ATP, so the P/O ratio is 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for FADH_2.

Cytoplasmic NADH enters by the malate–aspartate shuttle (heart, liver; 2.5 ATP each, total 32) or by the glycerol-phosphate shuttle (muscle, brain; 1.5 ATP each, total 30).

Part of the proton gradient is also spent on moving pyruvate and phosphate.

Conclusion. One glucose gives 30–32 ATP, about one-third of the 2870 kJ released by its complete oxidation being trapped; the rest escapes as heat, which keeps the body warm.
